planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring into rich, humus-heavy soil that never fully dries; 'Rotlaub' (German for 'red leaf') is prized for spring foliage that emerges a deeper, longer-lasting wine-red than most podophylla seedlings, an RHS Award of Garden Merit selection originally found at a Pacific Northwest botanic garden.

directions: Rotlaub carries the same duck-foot-shaped, deeply veined leaves typical of Rodgersia podophylla, but its new growth unfolds in a richer, more persistent red-bronze than the species, fading toward green only as summer heat sets in before some plants regain warm tones again in autumn. Creamy-white astilbe-like flower plumes rise on wiry stems in early summer, followed by decorative rust-red seed heads that extend interest into fall. Site it in a sheltered spot with constant moisture and morning sun to intensify the red coloring without scorching the large, thin leaves, and mulch heavily to buffer root temperature and retain soil moisture through summer. Divide congested clumps in early spring only occasionally, since rodgersias resent frequent disturbance.

planting.note: Set divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade with shelter from wind; 'Hercules' (also sold as 'Herkules') is among the largest-growing rodgersia selections, so allow generous room for its bold clump to mature over several seasons before crowding neighbors.

directions: Hercules lives up to its name with pleated, reddish-bronze basal foliage that expands into some of the largest leaves of any pinnata selection before greening in hot weather, and in summer it sends up branched, bottlebrush-like spikes of soft pink flowers well above the foliage mound. Its outsized scale makes it a dramatic anchor plant at a pond margin or the back of a large bog garden, where it pairs well with other bold-textured moisture lovers like ligularia and rodgersia relatives. Give it rich, constantly moist soil and protection from strong wind and hot afternoon sun, both of which quickly tatter and scorch the large, thin leaves. Divide only when clumps become congested, since established plants resent root disturbance and can take a full season to recover vigor.

common_name: Osiris Café Noir Ligularia (Dwarf Dark-Leaved Leopard Plant)

planting.note: Plant in spring in cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Osiris Cafe Noir' arose from a seedling of 'Othello' bred at Les Jardins Osiris in Quebec and stays notably more compact than most bigleaf ligularia cultivars, making it a better fit for smaller shaded beds.

directions: Osiris Cafe Noir produces incised, undulating, heart-shaped leaves that emerge deep purple-black and pass through bronze tones before settling to olive-green, with a red-purple underside that shows well when the leaves catch low light or a breeze. Clusters of bright yellow-orange daisy flowers open on dark stems in late summer into early fall, contrasting sharply with the dark foliage. Its compact, roughly two-foot habit makes it far easier to place in a modest shade border or container than full-sized dentata cultivars, though it shares the genus's dramatic midday wilting in heat and demands the same reliably damp, sheltered, cool-rooted site to look its best. Divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in deep, fertile, moisture-retentive soil in a sheltered spot with partial to full shade; 'Dark Beauty' holds its plum-purple foliage color especially well through the season compared with older dentata selections that tend to green up by midsummer.

directions: Dark Beauty forms a bold clump of large, serrated, rounded leaves that hold a deep plum-purple color on top with a curious plum-purple underside throughout the growing season, rather than fading toward green as many bigleaf ligularias do by midsummer. Bold panicles of bright yellow daisy flowers rise on dark stems from late summer into early fall, standing out sharply against the persistently dark foliage. Like other bigleaf ligularias it wilts visibly during hot afternoons even in adequately moist soil, recovering fully overnight, so give it a cool, sheltered position with dependable moisture and afternoon shade rather than treating the wilting as a sign of disease. Mulch to conserve soil moisture and divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to renew vigor.
